message:
QUESTION:
How much did the average-speed cameras reduce injury collisions at the 10 sites, and what would a city-wide rollout achieve?

DATA:
Average-speed cameras at 10 sites, installed January 2023. The 10 sites were chosen because they had the highest numbers of injury collisions in the city in 2020-2022.

| | 2020-2022 (3 years before) | 2023-2025 (3 years after) |
| Injury collisions at the 10 camera sites | 156 | 102 |
| Injury collisions on all other city roads | 3,600 | 3,240 |

Traffic: a bypass opened in March 2023 and diverted through-traffic away from 6 of the 10 sites. Traffic counts at the 10 sites fell by an average of 15% between the two periods. Traffic on other city roads was broadly unchanged.

Speed surveys at the camera sites (speed limit 30 mph): mean speed 34 mph before installation, 31 mph after.

The 10 sites are all urban arterial roads. The city has about 900 km of roads, of which the camera sites cover about 12 km. Most of the network is residential streets with low collision counts.

<analysis>
# Average-Speed Cameras: Three-Year Evaluation (Revised)

## Summary

Injury collisions at the 10 camera sites fell by 35%, from 156 to 102. After allowing for the city-wide trend, the fall is about 27%. That figure overstates what the cameras achieved, for two reasons:

- **The sites were picked for their unusually high 2020-2022 counts.** Some of the later fall would have happened anyway (regression to the mean).
- **A bypass opened in March 2023 and cut traffic at the sites by 15%.** Traffic on the comparison roads did not change.

Allowing for the traffic fall alone brings the estimated camera effect down to roughly 15%. That estimate is statistically uncertain and is still inflated by regression to the mean. The cameras probably helped. Mean speeds fell from 34 to 31 mph. But the data cannot tell us by how much.

The results do not support a forecast for a city-wide rollout. In particular, the draft's figure of about 290 collisions prevented a year should not be used.

## Background

Average-speed cameras were installed at 10 sites in January 2023. This note compares injury collisions over three full years before (2020-2022) and three full years after (2023-2025). It looks at the 10 sites and at all other city roads.

All 10 sites are urban arterial roads. Together they cover about 12 km of the city's 900 km network, about 1.3% of its length. They are much more collision-dense than the rest of the network:

- **Camera sites (before):** about 4.3 injury collisions per km per year (52 a year over 12 km).
- **All other roads:** about 1.35 per km per year (1,200 a year over 888 km).

## Raw change

| | 2020-2022 | 2023-2025 | Change |
|---|---|---|---|
| Camera sites | 156 (52/yr) | 102 (34/yr) | −35% |
| All other roads | 3,600 (1,200/yr) | 3,240 (1,080/yr) | −10% |

## Allowing for the background trend

The ratio of after to before at the sites is 0.654. On other roads it is 0.900. Dividing one by the other gives 0.727, a relative reduction of about 27%.

Put another way, the 10% background fall would have taken the sites from 52 to an expected 46.8 collisions a year. The observed figure is 34, a gap of about 13 a year.

This 27% is an upper-end estimate. Three problems mean the true camera effect is smaller, and less certain, than it suggests.

### 1. Regression to the mean

The sites were chosen because they had the city's highest injury-collision counts in 2020-2022. A site's count in any period reflects its underlying risk plus random variation. Sites picked for high counts will tend to have had bad luck in that period. Their counts would be expected to fall afterwards even if nothing changed.

The 2020-2022 period is therefore not a fair baseline. It is biased upwards, and part of the 35% fall is an artefact of how the sites were chosen. We cannot size this bias from the data here. Studies of speed-camera schemes have often found it to be a substantial share of the apparent effect.

To estimate it, we would need either:

- collision counts at the sites for earlier years (for example 2015-2019), or
- an empirical Bayes analysis using similar arterial roads without cameras.

### 2. The bypass reduced traffic at the sites

The bypass opened in March 2023 and diverted through-traffic away from 6 of the 10 sites. Average traffic at the sites fell by 15%. Traffic on the comparison roads was broadly unchanged. So the comparison roads do not account for this.

Assume, roughly, that collisions scale with traffic volume. Then the expected count without cameras is about 46.8 × 0.85 ≈ 39.8 a year, against 34 observed. That implies a camera effect of about 6 collisions a year, or roughly 15% (0.727 / 0.85 ≈ 0.855).

The relationship between traffic and collisions is not exactly proportional, so this is approximate. A site-by-site comparison would help: the 6 bypass-affected sites against the 4 unaffected ones.

### 3. Small numbers

The counts at the sites are small, so random variation matters. Treating the counts as Poisson gives approximate 95% intervals:

- **Unadjusted ratio of 0.727:** about 0.56 to 0.94, a reduction somewhere between 6% and 44%.
- **Traffic-adjusted ratio of about 0.855:** roughly 0.66 to 1.1. This is consistent with anything from a sizeable reduction to no effect.

Both intervals exist before any allowance for regression to the mean.

## Speeds

Speed surveys at the sites show mean speeds falling from 34 mph to 31 mph. That is a 3 mph reduction, which still leaves the mean slightly above the 30 mph limit.

A fall of this size is consistent with some real reduction in collision risk and severity. It is the clearest direct evidence that the cameras changed driver behaviour. However, the bypass may also have changed the traffic mix and speeds at the affected sites, so not all of the speed change can be credited to the cameras.

## City-wide rollout

The evaluation does not support an estimate of what a city-wide rollout would achieve. Applying a 27% reduction to all 1,080 collisions a year on other roads is not valid, for three reasons:

- **The 27% is itself overstated**, because of regression to the mean and the bypass.
- **It was measured on 12 km of high-collision arterial roads.** Most of the remaining 888 km is residential streets with low collision counts and different traffic conditions. Average-speed cameras are designed for corridors and are rarely suited to residential streets. There is no basis for assuming the same percentage effect there.
- **The benefit per camera falls steeply as you move to lower-risk roads.** Low collision counts mean few collisions to prevent per km, against similar installation and running costs.

Any extension should be framed as targeted deployment on other high-risk arterial corridors, not as a city-wide programme.

## Recommendations

1. **Do not fund a city-wide programme on the basis of this evaluation.**
2. **Re-analyse the existing sites before deciding on extension.** Specifically:
   - obtain pre-2020 collision data for the 10 sites, or carry out an empirical Bayes analysis, to estimate regression to the mean;
   - analyse the 6 bypass-affected and 4 unaffected sites separately;
   - use comparison sites of the same road type (arterials), not all other roads;
   - examine collision severity as well as counts.
3. **If the corrected effect remains worthwhile, pilot cameras on a small number of further high-risk arterial corridors.** Design the pilot so it can be evaluated properly, for example with comparable control corridors and baselines that are not the same years used for site selection.
4. **Continue annual monitoring** of collisions and speeds at the original 10 sites.

## Costs and publication

Average-speed camera systems carry installation, maintenance and enforcement costs. A business case for any extension should set these against a corrected estimate of the collisions prevented, valued by severity. The evaluation, including its limitations, should be published so residents can see the results.

---

## Main changes from the draft

- **Speed figure corrected.** The data show the mean falling to 31 mph, not 26 mph. That is still above the 30 mph limit, not "well below" it.
- **Site selection.** The draft called the 2020-2022 baseline "fair". Because the sites were chosen for their high counts in that period, the baseline is biased upwards (regression to the mean).
- **Bypass added.** The draft ignored the bypass, which cut traffic at the sites by 15% but not on the comparison roads. Adjusting for it roughly halves the estimated effect, to about 15%.
- **Uncertainty quantified.** I added approximate statistical intervals. After the traffic adjustment, they do not rule out no effect.
- **City-wide claim removed.** The draft applied a 27% cut to the whole network, giving about 290 collisions a year. I removed this, because the result comes from 12 km of high-risk arterials and most of the network is low-collision residential streets.
- **Recommendation changed.** It now calls for a corrected analysis and targeted, well-evaluated extension instead of city-wide funding.
- **Arithmetic retained.** The draft's arithmetic (35%, 10%, 0.727, 46.8 vs 34) was correct and is kept.
</analysis>

<review>
# Review of the Average-Speed Camera Evaluation

The analysis is sound, and I'd endorse its conclusions. The arithmetic checks out, the three main threats to validity are correctly identified, and the city-wide forecast is rightly withdrawn. A few points could be sharpened.

## Arithmetic

I recomputed every figure, and all are correct:

| Figure | Check |
|---|---|
| Sites: 156 → 102 | ratio 0.654, −35% ✓ |
| Other roads: 3,600 → 3,240 | ratio 0.900, −10% ✓ |
| Relative ratio | 0.654 / 0.900 = 0.727 ✓ |
| Expected vs observed | 52 × 0.9 = 46.8 vs 34 ✓ |
| Traffic-adjusted | 46.8 × 0.85 = 39.8; 34 / 39.8 = 0.855 ✓ |
| Collision density | 52/12 = 4.3; 1,200/888 = 1.35 per km per year ✓ |
| 95% interval, unadjusted | SE(log ratio) ≈ 0.130 gives 0.56–0.94 ✓ |
| 95% interval, traffic-adjusted | 0.66–1.10 ✓ |
| Draft's city-wide figure | 0.27 × 1,080 ≈ 290 ✓ (correctly rejected) |

## What the analysis gets right

- **Regression to the mean.** It correctly says this bias exists here and cannot be sized from the data. It names the right fixes: earlier baseline years, or an empirical Bayes analysis.
- **The bypass.** It spots this confounder and notes that the comparison roads don't account for it.
- **Uncertainty.** It shows that after the traffic adjustment, "no effect" is within the plausible range.
- **Speeds.** It corrects the speed claim: 31 mph is still above the limit.
- **City-wide rollout.** It rejects extrapolation to the whole network for the right reasons: different road types, a corridor-specific technology, and lower benefit per km on low-risk roads.

## Suggested improvements

1. **Say which way the traffic adjustment errs.** Assuming collisions scale one-for-one with traffic is approximate. In most studies, collisions rise less than proportionally with traffic. If that holds here, the 15% adjustment over-corrects. The camera effect before allowing for regression to the mean would then sit somewhere between about 15% and 27%, not at 15%. The opposite case is also possible: if the bypass removed mainly heavy through-traffic, the safety benefit could exceed the volume change. It's worth stating both possibilities explicitly.

2. **Use the speed data as a cross-check.** Established speed–collision models (e.g. Nilsson's Power Model) predict that injury collisions change roughly with the square of mean speed. On that basis, (31/34)² ≈ 0.83, a reduction of about 17%. This is independent support for an effect in the mid-teens. It strengthens the "cameras probably helped" conclusion without leaning on the confounded collision counts. The same caveat applies, since the bypass may have affected speeds too.

3. **Note the COVID-19 period.** The 2020–2022 baseline includes pandemic years with unusual traffic volumes and speeds. Those years may have affected arterial roads differently from residential streets. This adds further doubt about whether "all other roads" is a valid comparison. It supports the existing recommendation to use comparison sites of the same road type.

4. **Show the 15% average is a simplification.** The 15% traffic fall is an average over 10 sites, but the bypass affected only 6 of them. The recommended split into bypass-affected and unaffected sites is the right fix. A one-line note that the average hides this variation would help readers.

5. **Check the "changes from the draft" section.** It refers to a draft that isn't included here, such as the 26 mph figure. I couldn't verify those claims. Make sure that section matches the draft before circulating.

## Bottom line

On the question asked, the analysis gives a defensible answer:

- **Effect at the 10 sites:** the cameras probably reduced injury collisions there, plausibly by something in the order of 10–20%. The data cannot pin this down, and regression to the mean has not yet been removed.
- **City-wide rollout:** the evaluation provides no valid basis for estimating its effect.

The recommendations follow logically from these findings: re-analyse, then pilot a targeted, properly evaluated extension. Only minor additions are needed.
</review>

# Receipt

The review accepts the analysis's arithmetic and conclusions. I re-checked its own checks, and they hold. For example, SE(log ratio) = √(1/156 + 1/102 + 1/3,600 + 1/3,240) ≈ 0.130, which gives intervals of 0.56–0.94 and 0.66–1.10. It makes five suggestions.

1. **Say which way the traffic adjustment errs.** The analysis assumes collisions fall one-for-one with traffic. Most evidence suggests collisions change less than proportionally with traffic. If so, the bypass explains less of the fall, and the camera effect (before allowing for regression to the mean) sits between about 15% and 27%, not at 15%. The opposite is possible if the bypass removed mainly heavy through-traffic. **Change:** present the traffic adjustment as a range and state both directions.

2. **Use the speeds as a cross-check.** The Power Model says injury collisions scale roughly with the square of mean speed: (31/34)² ≈ 0.83, about a 17% reduction. This supports a mid-teens effect without relying on the confounded collision counts. The caveat is that the bypass may also have changed speeds. **Change:** add this estimate to the Speeds section and the summary.
   - The review doesn't mention one extra strength, which I've added: the speed evidence is not distorted by regression to the mean, because the sites were selected on collisions, not speeds.

3. **Note the COVID-19 period.** The 2020–2022 baseline includes pandemic years with unusual traffic and speeds. These may have affected arterials differently from residential streets. **Change:** add this as a further threat to the baseline. It also strengthens the recommendation to use arterial comparison sites.

4. **Flag that the 15% traffic fall is an average.** The bypass affected only 6 of the 10 sites, so the average hides variation. **Change:** add a one-line note. The existing recommendation (split the sites into affected and unaffected) already addresses it.

5. **Check the "changes from the draft" section.** It refers to a draft that isn't provided, such as the 26 mph figure, so it can't be verified. **Change:** keep the section but mark it as needing checking against the draft before circulation.

One point where I depart slightly from the review: its bottom line, "plausibly 10–20%", is a little more precise than the evidence allows. The adjusted intervals include no effect, and regression to the mean is unquantified. I state a plausible range but keep "unproven" alongside it.

# Average-Speed Cameras: Three-Year Evaluation (Revised)

## Summary

- **The sites were picked for their unusually high 2020–2022 counts.** Some of the later fall would have happened anyway (regression to the mean).
- **A bypass opened in March 2023 and cut traffic at the sites by 15%.** Traffic on the comparison roads did not change.

Allowing for the traffic fall gives a camera effect of roughly **15–21%**. The low end assumes collisions fall in proportion to traffic. The high end assumes, more realistically, that they fall less than proportionally. The speed data point the same way: mean speeds fell from 34 to 31 mph, and standard speed–collision models predict about a 17% reduction in injury collisions from that change.

These estimates still include an unknown amount of regression to the mean. They are also statistically uncertain: at the lower end, the plausible range includes no effect. **The cameras probably reduced injury collisions modestly, but the size of the effect is not established.**

The results do not support a forecast for a city-wide rollout. In particular, the draft's figure of about 290 collisions prevented a year should not be used.

## Background

Average-speed cameras were installed at 10 sites in January 2023. This note compares injury collisions over three full years before (2020–2022) and three full years after (2023–2025). It looks at the 10 sites and at all other city roads.

All 10 sites are urban arterial roads. Together they cover about 12 km of the city's 900 km network, about 1.3% of its length. They are much more collision-dense than the rest of the network:

- **Camera sites (before):** about 4.3 injury collisions per km per year (52 a year over 12 km).
- **All other roads:** about 1.35 per km per year (1,200 a year over 888 km).

## Raw change

| | 2020–2022 | 2023–2025 | Change |
|---|---|---|---|
| Camera sites | 156 (52/yr) | 102 (34/yr) | −35% |
| All other roads | 3,600 (1,200/yr) | 3,240 (1,080/yr) | −10% |

## Allowing for the background trend

The ratio of after to before at the sites is 0.654. On other roads it is 0.900. Dividing one by the other gives 0.727, a relative reduction of about 27%.

### 1. Regression to the mean

To estimate it, we would need either:

- collision counts at the sites for earlier years (for example 2015–2019), or
- an empirical Bayes analysis using similar arterial roads without cameras.

### 2. The bypass reduced traffic at the sites

The bypass diverted through-traffic away from 6 of the 10 sites. Average traffic at the sites fell by 15%, while traffic on the comparison roads was broadly unchanged. So the comparison roads do not account for this.

The 15% is an average. The fall was presumably concentrated at the 6 affected sites, with little change at the other 4.

How much of the collision fall the bypass explains depends on how collisions respond to traffic volume:

| Assumption | Traffic factor | Expected without cameras (per yr) | Camera ratio | Camera effect |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Collisions unaffected by traffic | 1.00 | 46.8 | 0.727 | ~27% |
| Collisions ∝ traffic^0.5 | 0.922 | 43.1 | 0.789 | ~21% |
| Collisions ∝ traffic (proportional) | 0.85 | 39.8 | 0.855 | ~15% |

Most road-safety models find that collisions rise less than proportionally with traffic. This makes the 15–21% range more plausible than 15% alone.

The adjustment could err the other way, though. If the bypass mainly removed heavy through-traffic, its safety benefit could exceed the volume change, and the camera effect would be below 15%.

A site-by-site comparison of the 6 bypass-affected sites against the 4 unaffected ones would narrow this down.

### 3. The COVID-19 baseline

The 2020–2022 baseline includes pandemic years with unusual traffic volumes and speeds. These conditions may have affected arterial roads differently from residential streets. This casts further doubt on whether "all other roads", which are mostly residential, is a valid comparison group. The direction of the resulting bias is unclear.

### 4. Small numbers

The counts at the sites are small, so random variation matters. Treating the counts as Poisson gives approximate 95% intervals:

- **Unadjusted ratio of 0.727:** about 0.56 to 0.94, a reduction somewhere between 6% and 44%.
- **Proportional traffic adjustment (ratio 0.855):** about 0.66 to 1.10. This is consistent with anything from a sizeable reduction to no effect.

Both intervals exist before any allowance for regression to the mean.

## Speeds

Speed surveys at the sites show mean speeds falling from 34 mph to 31 mph. That is a 3 mph reduction, which still leaves the mean slightly above the 30 mph limit. It is the clearest direct evidence that the cameras changed driver behaviour.

The speed change also gives an independent estimate of the effect. Nilsson's Power Model predicts that injury collisions change roughly with the square of mean speed. On that basis, (31/34)² ≈ 0.83, about a 17% reduction, which sits within the 15–21% range above.

This cross-check has two advantages over the collision counts:

- It does not depend on the choice of comparison roads.
- It is not distorted by regression to the mean, because the sites were selected on collision counts, not speeds.

It has one limitation. The bypass may have changed the traffic mix and speeds at the 6 affected sites, so not all of the speed fall can be credited to the cameras.

## City-wide rollout

The evaluation does not support an estimate of what a city-wide rollout would achieve. Applying a 27% reduction to all 1,080 collisions a year on other roads is not valid, for three reasons:

- **The 27% is overstated**, because of the bypass and regression to the mean.
- **It was measured on 12 km of high-collision arterial roads.** Most of the remaining 888 km is residential streets with low collision counts and different traffic conditions. 1. **Do not fund a city-wide programme on the basis of this evaluation.**
2. **Re-analyse the existing sites before deciding on extension.** Specifically:
   - obtain pre-2020 collision data for the 10 sites, or carry out an empirical Bayes analysis, to estimate regression to the mean (pre-2020 data also gives a baseline unaffected by COVID-19);
   - analyse the 6 bypass-affected and 4 unaffected sites separately, using site-level traffic counts;
   - use comparison sites of the same road type (arterials), not all other roads;
   - examine collision severity as well as counts, and repeat the speed–collision cross-check at the 4 unaffected sites.
3. **If the corrected effect remains worthwhile, pilot cameras on a small number of further high-risk arterial corridors.** Design the pilot so it can be evaluated properly, with comparable control corridors and baselines that are not the same years used for site selection.
4. **Continue annual monitoring** of collisions and speeds at the original 10 sites.

## Costs and publication

Average-speed camera systems carry installation, maintenance and enforcement costs. A business case for any extension should set these against a corrected estimate of the collisions prevented, valued by severity. The evaluation, including its limitations, should be published so residents can see the results.

## Main changes from the draft

*The draft is not reproduced in this note. Check the items below against it before circulating.*

- **Speed figure corrected.** The data show the mean falling to 31 mph, not 26 mph. That is still above the 30 mph limit, not "well below" it.
- **Site selection.** The draft called the 2020–2022 baseline "fair". Because the sites were chosen for their high counts in that period, the baseline is biased upwards (regression to the mean). It also covers the COVID-19 period.
- **Bypass added.** The draft ignored the bypass, which cut traffic at the sites by 15% but not on the comparison roads. Adjusting for it reduces the estimated effect to roughly 15–21%, depending on how collisions respond to traffic.
- **Speed–collision cross-check added.** The Power Model gives about 17%, consistent with the adjusted range.
- **Uncertainty quantified.** I added approximate statistical intervals. With the full traffic adjustment, they do not rule out no effect.
- **City-wide claim removed.** The draft applied a 27% cut to the whole network, giving about 290 collisions a year. I removed this because the result comes from 12 km of high-risk arterials, while most of the network is low-collision residential streets.
- **Recommendation changed.** It now calls for a corrected analysis and a targeted, well-evaluated extension instead of city-wide funding.
- **Arithmetic retained.** The draft's arithmetic (35%, 10%, 0.727, 46.8 vs 34) was correct and is kept.
